title: Arc sistrum with a hymn to Hathor

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A tall, narrow faience object with a handle below and a rounded arch above, an ancient Egyptian rattle called a sistrum. Columns of hieroglyphs are carved or marked on its surface.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, date, medium, period, dimensions, tags (Hieroglyphs, Goddess), public-domain flag, credit line and image URLs read from the record

context: A faience sistrum, a kind of ritual rattle, from Egypt's Ptolemaic Period (332–30 BCE). The record's title says it carries a hymn to the goddess Hathor, and its tags mention hieroglyphs. It stands about 39.4 cm tall and about 10 cm wide.

descriptions.k: This is a rattle from ancient Egypt, called a sistrum. It has a handle and a big arch on top. Writing covers it. People shook rattles like this to make music for a goddess named Hathor.
descriptions.g12: A sistrum was a rattle that people in ancient Egypt shook during religious ceremonies. This one has a handle and a curved arch, and its surface has hieroglyphs, the picture writing of Egypt. The words are a hymn, a song of praise, to the goddess Hathor. What sound do you imagine it made?
descriptions.g35: This sistrum is a musical rattle from ancient Egypt, made of faience between 332 and 30 BCE. It has a handle at the bottom and an arch on top, shaped so that rods or other noisemakers could have been attached. Hieroglyphs on it carry a hymn to Hathor, a goddess linked with music and joy. Why would the writing be on the instrument itself?
descriptions.g68: Sistra were used in Egyptian worship, especially for goddesses such as Hathor, who was linked with music, joy, and love. This faience arc sistrum has a handle and a graceful curve, and it carries a hymn in hieroglyphs. The object combines sound, image, and text in one form. Faience is fragile, so we might wonder whether it was used or made as an offering. What clues in the shape suggest its function?
descriptions.g910: This Ptolemaic sistrum merges instrument, inscription, and devotional object. The arc form, tall handle, and surface of hieroglyphs make it both a musical device and a vehicle for words addressed to Hathor. Faience's delicacy suggests it may have been used in ritual or dedicated as an offering, though the record does not settle this. How does the combination of shape and text shape our sense of the object's role?
descriptions.g1112: The arc sistrum with a hymn to Hathor is a compact example of how Egyptian ritual objects braid together sound, text, and image. The curved frame and handle identify the type, while the hieroglyphic hymn names a goddess associated with music, joy, and motherhood. Its faience material raises questions about use: a fragile surface seems at odds with vigorous shaking, so it may have been votive. Such tensions remind us that museum labels reduce complex practices, and interpretation requires comparing form, inscription, and context.

teacherNote.context: A Ptolemaic faience sistrum inscribed with a hymn to the goddess Hathor. Sistra were rattles used in Egyptian ritual, and this fragile example may have been made as an offering.
directions: Have students invent a rattle design and decide what words or symbols to put on it.
Ask students to compare what we can learn from an inscription with what we can learn from shape alone.
Discuss how an instrument can be an object of devotion as well as a source of sound.
